SPOKANE FALLS, May 23, 1882. — A railroad accident of a peculiar nature occurred about three miles east of here yesterday. The east bound train consisting of about twenty-seven freight, one passenger and express car, became uncoupled about the forward portion and becoming considerably ahead before the engineer noticed the separation and thinking the rear end of the train was stationary backed up, but it so happened that the rest of the train was on a down grade and running at full speed. The collision was terrible, eleven cars being piled on top of one another and broken to splinters. A brakeman named M. E. Sancey was taken from the debris in an insensible condition and brought to this city; it was thought he was fatally injured, but there are hopes of his recovery to-day. None of the passengers sustained any injury beyond a good shaking up, theirs being the last coach. A fireman on the railroad named John Ringwood got killed on Sunday last at Sandy Point by being accidently run over by an engine.

WALA WALA (W. T.) May 25th - A
Summary Punishment Meted Out to a Petty Offender.

WALLA WALLA (W. T.). May 25th.—A year since a family named Neal lived at Rockford, Spokan county. They were known as a tough set—a sort of Younger family on a small scale. One of them was indicted for creating a disturbance at the Methodist church and arraigned at the District Court. He succeeded in getting a continuance, and in the meantime the family pulled up stakes and journeyed to Montana, and their going was a signal for rejoicing among the law-abiding settlers in that section. Aldy, one of the boys, and a sister remained, and in November last this man was arrested for stealing a horse; but he left the country and joined the family in Montana. Last Sunday he again appeared at Rockford, coming, as he said, for his sister. Once housed, a party of citizens, knowing that he was wanted, surrounded the house and captured him. A detail of citizens was made to convey him to Cheney, and as threats of lynching had been made, the detail started at daylight on Monday; but when about a mile and a half from Rockford, and while passing a thick growth of timber, about twenty men heavily armed and the lower part of their faces masked, stepped into the roadway before and behind the guard, and under cocked revolvers forced them to deliver up the prisoner. Two men then unstrapped Neal from the saddle he was bound on and led him into the timber. Realizing his position he begged piteously for his life, promising that he would confess all the wrong himself and family had ever done in the neighborhood, and would leave the place forever. The captors paid no heed, but told him his time had come and he had better make peace with his Creator. They gave him a minute for preparation, and then fastened a stout rope about his neck, and throwing it over a limb, several men caught it, and Andy Neal was swinging between heaven and earth. After the crowd had become satisfied that he was dead, all separated and rode off. Those who first arrested Neal say that they cannot identify any of the lynchers. Walla Walla condemns the affair, and says that Neal was a bad man in a petty way only, and that a severe cowhiding would have cured him of his devilty and frightened him out of the country.

A BLOODY AFFRAY.

SAN FRANCISCO, May 25.—The Tombstone Epitaph publishes an account of a fight at Igos ranche, on the line of the Arizona & New Mexico railroad, near the Sonora border. Much ill feeling had arisen beween American railroad laborers and Mexicans. A few evenings ago a number of Mexicans with their families encamped near Igos ranche. The American laborers, being drunk, attempted to force Mexicans to give up their women. This was resisted and an affray followed in which seven Mexicans were killed and several wounded. A number of Americans were wounded, and it is thought they will die.

KILLED BY FALLING ROCK.

NEW YORK, May 25.—In a new tunnel in the process of excavation through the Palisades, at Union Hill, New Jersey, for the New York, Ontario & Western railway, several tons of rock fell to-day upon the workmen. Two were killed and another probably fatally injured. Work was suspended for the time.

BOSTON, May 25.—At Marlboro, Massachusetts, yesterday afternoon, Lewis Targe, champion bycicle rider of the United States, was thrown from his bicycle and had his skull fractured. He will probably die.

Collingwood, Ont., May 25.—It is now learned that fourteen person lost their lives by drowning from the steamer Manitowec, in Lake Huron, last week. The fire was caused by the explosion of a coal oil lamp.

THE KNIFE.

KNOXVILLE, May 25.—Yesterday, near House Mountain, sixteen miles from Knoxville, John Walker was stabbed by Andrew Evans. Walker, who had been carrying a sack of meal, picked it up, walked two hundred yards, fell, and died in four minutes. Evans gave himself up last night and is now in jail.

On Sunday-night, says the Standard, a party of citizens in the vicinity of Rockport, thirty-five miles east of Cheney, W. T., surrounded the house in which Aldey Neil, a well-known and desperate horse thief, was stopping, and after considerable parley he agreed to surrender if they would give him a trial. Messrs. Starr, Henderson and Gilbert were selected to take him to Cheney. They had proceeded with him some eight miles, when a band of masked men sprang from the woods, surrounded the hack, and after the exchange of a few shots between the guards and lynchers, Neil was given up. He was taken to a tree, and when daybreak came his lifeless body was there found. The lynchers then proceeded in search of another thief, William McCane, who escaped from the Cheney jail in April, with what success is not learned. Neil was a desperate character. He was last fall captured with seventy-five head of stolen horses, but escaped from the guard. He shouted to his guard just before the lynching that he feared neither God, man or the devil.

A planter in Rapides Parish, La., cultivated one thousand acres of cotton last year, and four hundred acres in Bermuda grass. The cotton yielded him a net return of about $1,000 less than the grass. The cotton was cultivated with severe manual labor, while the grass was handled entirely by machinery.

A negro boy recently threw his top through a store window in Selma, Ala. As soon as he laid hands on the offending toy, he grasped it with steel spinner outward, and beat himself fiercely over the forehead and head with it until blood came, when he threw the top as far away as he could and told the owner of the store that he "didn't go to break the window." This was a novel way of atoning for his fault, but it had the desired effect and he was allowed to depart unmolested.

The manufacture of canes and curiosities is one of the leading industries of Jacksonville, Fla., furnishing employment to a greater number of persons than any other branch of business in the city. Almost every thing in the shape of fish, flesh or fowl, animal, mineral or vegetable, is manufactured into articles of jewelry, for personal use or adornment. The trade in alligators is also large. One concern has sold over eight hundred alligators this season, and another over five hundred within a month.

One hundred citizens of Tuscaloosa County, Alabama, have been taken to Montgomery to give bond to appear at the May term of the United States Court, for capturing a few lightwood knots and a few trees standing and lying idle on some of Uncle Sam's $20 per acre mineral lands. No "favors" shown—the Marshal just cleans them up for the money there is in it.

The country contiguous to Vicksburg, Miss., is now almost entirely out of water, and planting and plowing is becoming general. The prospect for the Hill City is unusually good. A full crop will be made, and the people are alive with the hope that comes of the best prospects.

Eight hundred and twenty-three needles and pins have been cut out of Miss Stokes, a very intelligent young lady living ten miles west of Moulton, Ala., within the past few years. She declares that she does not swallow or stick them in her herself, and it is very mysterious how the pins get buried in her body, causing great pain and vexation of spirit.

There are 5,000,000 sheep in Texas.

A Mormon church has been established in Sevier County, Arkansas, with several members, among the most ignorant class of people. One preacher was run out of the county, but two others have appeared. They profess to be opposed to polygamy.

A gentleman and two ladies went to Brunswick from St. Simons, Ga., in a row boat, and on the way back got into a creek and were left by the tide in a marsh. MANSFIELD, O., April 29, 1882. Yesterday the suit of the Standard Mutual Lite Insurance Company, of Mansfield, Ohio, to revoke its charter, was heard in the Supreme Court, and some thirty witnesses examined. ROCHESTER, May 31.—A report comes from Dover Center that Frank Radlidge, sixteen years old, committed an outrage on Minnie Harvey, four years of age. Radlidge enticed her into a granary near Harvey's house and made the assault there. Mrs. Harvey, hearing a noise, opened the granary door and saw Frank in the act, holding his hand over Minnie's mouth to stifle her cries for help. As soon as he was discovered he fled. In a short time a crowd was hunting him with the full intent of lynching him, but he eluded them and effected his escape. Minnie was seriously injured and was confined to her bed several days.

A FEARLESS STAND.
The course taken by the Tribune in speaking fearlessly of existing evils has not only attracted general attention, but has met with hearty approval from all classes of citizens.

Not only from ladies and business men have the kind words come, but particularly from the laboring men, who realize that whatever retards improvement in the city reduces their chances for securing employment and cuts the price of labor. They realize that the construction of a dozen brick blocks in Bismarck this summer would afford bread and clothing for wife and babies and give good cheer to many families.

The property-holders realize that a boom for Bismarck means a largely increased value for their homes, with pride and independence that the oppressed can never feel.

All realize that the improvement of the city will attract attention to the country. That the settlement of the country will build up the city. That to build up the city we must gain, not additional saloons and gambling halls, but manufacturing interests. We must make the city attractive for families. A thousand men employed on the river would make Bismarck "red hot" on the day of the arrival of each boat: Pay day at the Fort has a very exhilarating effect, also, but of how much greater value would be the settlement of a thousand families of men engaged in manufacturing. A thousand families of men engaged in tilling the soil; in growing wheat and cattle; in making butter and cheese and producing other necessaries of life will be worth a thousand times more to Bismarck than a perfect jam of miners, bullwhackers and negro rousters.

Schools and churches will be worth far more than palaces of sin. Other things have been demanded by the class that concentrated at Bismarck during the days when it was the terminus; when it was the outfitting point for the Black Hills; when keno and the rattling of poker chips was heard on every hand; but those days are over, and every good citizen ought to rejoice that it is so, and that a day of better things is being ushered in.

The TRIBUNE repeats there is no point in the west, or in the east, in the south or in the north, on the North Pacific or on any other railroad on the face of the earth better located than Bismarck. The site is all that could be desired. Millions would not put Fargo or Mandan in as good condition as that of Bismarek, so far as drainage is concerned. Thousands would be required to make their streets as good as nature has made those of Bismarck.

It is only necessary to make capital feel that this is a safe point for investment and encourage families to believe that here society will be protected and the best possible facilities afforded for the education of our children. Then the city will indeed begin to prosper. The day has come when this can be done. Let those abundantly able to build follow the example set by the banks, and it will not long be said that Bismarck is the only town on the line of the North Pacific that does not show signs of solid prosperity.

The Banner City, which was published recently for distribution among land seekers, in speaking of the climate of Bismarck, says:

The climate of Bismarck and its surroundings is very different from, and vastly better than that of Fargo and the country for a long distance east of it. The former is situated in the most favored part of the Upper Missouri Valley, while the latter occupies a very objectionable position in the Valley of the Red River of the North. The former great Valley is a part of the Southern or Gulf system, and the latter, a part of the Northern or Hudson Bay system.

The characteristics of these two systems are as different and marked as the difference in the direction of their drainage. The waters of the one run South and those of the other run North; these commence their thawing, and flooding the country at their sources, at the first approaches of warm weather in the spring, and as it proceeds Northward the floods impeded by the ice, increase in volume until the whole valley is submurged, while those but a short distance below remain unfrozen and navigable all winter and when warm weather and thawing proceeds North the lower portion is first freed from ice and obstruction allowing the Spring floods to escape gradually and with comparatively little damage or disaster.

To the Gulf system belongs the genial south winds, accompanied by copious showers during the growing season, and in the upper portion of the Missouri Valley the winters are greatly modified by the warm air, heated by the Japan current of warm water in the Pacific Ocean, floating eastward until obstructed by the water shed dividing or separating the two systems; while the broad expanse of low and level land which characterizes the Northern system allows the cold blasts from Hudson Bay, a region of almost perpetual ice, to flow southward, accompanied with its cold rains in summer and mountains of snow in the winter. Still it grows good wheat, but is too cold for corn.

The Missouri Valley at Bismarck has an elevation of about 900 feet greater than the Red River Valley at Fargo.

The former is rolling and picturesque, while the latter is flat and monotonous.

Their lands are equally productive of the cereals, but for Indian corn and all varieties of esculent roots, the former has a decided advantage.

For purity of water, salubrity of climate, and beauty of scenery, the former has a greater comparative elevation over the latter than that of her elevation above the sea level. Still the latter is a wonderfully productive wheat country. But, while it is so, the former is equally productive with a thousand other equally desirable advantages.

ARREST OF THE ALLEGED PERPETRATOR.

Last evening information was received at police headquarters that a horrible outrage had been committed yesterday morning on the person of Mrs. Jennie Thomas, a married lady, living near Licksville, Frederick county, Md., a short distance beyond Point of Rocks, by a colored man about 24 years old, named James Carroll. It was thought that he had made his way to this District, and a full description of the suspected party was telephoned to the police precinct with an order to the officers to keep a sharp lookout. Last night about 11½ o'clock Officer B. F. Harper, of the Georgetown precinct, noticed a man coming down Bridge street at Frederick street, and arrested him on suspicion. On taking him to the station it was found that he answered in every particular the description given of the perpetrator of the outrage, excepting in name, he persisting that his name was Adam Austin and not James Carroll. He was, this morning, taken to police head quarters, and the Maryland authorities were notified. The officers feel certain that they have the perpetrator of the outrage. The man claims that he is innocent; that he has not been near the scene of the occurrence for some days; that he is a hand on the canal boat Mattle, which arrived here several days since, and had been in Georgetown four or five days.
frederick-prisoner-point-of-rocks.A3:
The Licksville, Md., Outrage.
Last evening two residents of Licksville, Frederick county, Md., arrived here to take a look at the colored man Adam Austin, who was arrested the previous night by Officer B. F. Harper in Georgetown, on suspicion of being the party who outraged Mrs. Jennie Thomas on Monday morning. They took a look at Austin, and deciding that he was not the man the prisoner was released.

The Baltimore Sun has a special from Frederick as to the occurrence, which refers to a letter received by Mr. John C. Motter, state's attorney for Frederick county, from Mr. Richard Thomas, dated Lickville, Frederick county, April 15, which says: "I write to say that a negro named James Carroll committed an outrage on the person of my wife last night during my absence from home, and I am advised to write to you as the proper person to prosecute the case. Carroll had on when he left here an old slouch hat without a band, new pair of pants and a run-down pair of shoes. He is of medium size, and has a rather repulsive-looking countenance. Use every effort in your power to have him arrested, for, besides the outrage, he has left my wife in a very precarious condition from severe choking and fright."

The following additional particulars have been gathered:—On Monday night the greater portion of the male population of Licksville were attending a ball given in the village in celebration of the Easter holidays. Mr. Thomas was on a visit to Point of Rocks. Taking advantage of these circumstances the negro Carroll first committed a robbery in the house of Mr. P. N. Leaplly, and then at about 11 o'clock proceeded to the residence of Mr. Thomas. After effecting an entrance through a window he broke open the door leading to the chamber of Mrs. Thomas, and, brandishing a huge knife, threatened the lady's life if she made the least outcry or resistance. In this manner the diabolical purpose of the flend was accomplished, Mrs. Thomas is a small, delicate woman, aged about 32 years, and the mother of five or six children. She is the daughter of Thomas Trundle, a prominent and highly respected farmer living near Licksville. The husband is a son of the late Captain Richard Thomas, who was a well-known citizen of this county. As soon as the outrage became known in the village the greatest excitement and indignation was aroused, and almost immediately more than fifty armed men began scouring the country in search of the villian. Up to this time, however, he has eluded arrest. If caught, it is thought he will certainly be lynched. Carroll was formerly employed on the canal as a boatman, and is about 22 years of age.

ARREST OF THE ALLEGED PERPETRATOR.

To-day about noon Carroll was discovered in Georgetown in the canal office by Officer Volkman, and he made an attempt to arrest him, when he ran, but was run down. He was taken to the station, and Lieutenant Skippon telegraphed the fact to headquarters. Besides corresponding exactly with the description given, he was fully identified by Mr. Thomas, the husband of the victim. He, however, asserted his innocence, and expressed a readiness to go to Frederick for trial, and he was delivered into the hands of the Maryland authorities.

The Arrest and Lynching of James Carroll.

James Carroll, the negro who outraged Mrs. Richard Thomas at Lickville, Frederick County, Maryland, last Monday night, was arrested in Georgetown at noon yesterday and was hanged by a lynching party near SugarLoaf Mountain, Maryland, while being taken to Frederick County last evening.

About noon yesterday Carroll was discovered walking on the tow-path of the canal, near Fayette street, Georgetown, by Mr. Richard Thomas, the husband of the outraged woman, who came to the city for the purpose of looking at the man named Adam Austin, who was arrested last Wednesday. Carroll passed Thomas and tipped his hat to him. Thomas immediately summoned Officer Volkman. Upon the appearance of the officer Carroll broke into a run, and taking a circuitous route through Water and Fayette streets returned to the tow-path of the canal, hotly pursued by the officer. At the Aqueduct Bridge the fugitive was stopped by Mr. Frizzell. Carroll showed resistance, but Mr. Frizzell held him until Officer Volkman came up, when he was turned over to the officer. He was then taken to the station-house and locked up. Carroll was very boastful and did not seem at all frightened. He made no attempt to conceal his identity. Some pieces of cloth torn from his clothing by Mrs. Thomas, which Mr. Thomas had in his possession, were found to correspond with rents in his clothing. Carroll was about twenty-one years of age, copper colored, of medium height, slender build, and very repulsive in appearance. He told the officers at the station that he ran away from Maryland because he knew he would be hung is he remained there. He said that, as he had to die only once, he was willing to return and suffer the penalty. When he was taken from the station-house a large crowd was collected about the doorway and there was considerable excitement. No attempt was made to interfere with the officers. One person remarked, however, that if they would take the prisoner back by way of the canal instead of the railroad he would guarantee that a rope would be ready for him by the time he reached the Chain Bridge. The prisoner was handcuffed and taken to the Baltimore and Ohio depot by Officers Volkman and Ben Harper. These officers left with him for Frederick County on the 4:35 train, and were accompanied by Mr. Thomas.

THE LYNCHING.

[Special to the National Republican.]

POINT OF ROCKS, Md., April 17.—The greatest excitement prevails in this vicinity over the lynching of James Carroll, the negro arrested in Washington for outraging Mrs. Richard Thomas at Licksville, Md. The news of his arrest reached this place this afternoon and arrangements were made deliberately to take the prisoner from the officers and lynch him upon his arrival here. Since the outrage was committed the excitement has been very great.

The train bringing Carroll arrived at 6:15 this evening. Some time before the arrival of the train crowds of men collected about the station. There was no mistaking their purpose. Upon the arrival of the train the men boarded it in small parties, as if they were passengers. These men got into the same car with the police officers and the prisoner. The train moved on.

At Sugar-Loaf Mountain, when a preconcerted signal was given, some of the crowd pounced upon the officers from behind, and a masked party, numbering fifteen or twenty, entered the car, bringing a rope. The officers resisted desperately, but were soon overpowered. The prisoner was wrested from them, and a rope placed around his neck.

Carroll begged piteously for mercy. He was dragged from the train and pulled across a field a distance of 100 yards or more to a spot known as Snaky Hollow. A tree most conveniently formed by nature for the purpose was found. Carroll, who was frantic with terror, implored his captors to spare him, but his prayers had no other effect than to make them more expeditious. The rope was thrown over a limb and the doomed man was hoisted into the air. He struggled desperately to free himself from the rope, but soon became quiet.
The lynchers remained on the spot until sure that the negro was dead, and then, mounting their horses, which were ready for them, rode silently away. No attempt was made to interfere with them. The whole operation, from the time the train was boarded until the lifeless body of Carroll was left dangling on the tree, occupied only about thirty minutes on the tree, occupied only about thirty minutes. The body was left on the tree over an hour, when it was cut down by direction of the county officers. An inquest will be held to-morrow, when the police officers and others who came on the train from Washington will probably be called as witnesses.

POINT OF ROCKS, (Metropolitan Branch B. & O. R. R.,) April 18th, 1879.—James Carroll, the negro ravisher of Mrs. Jennie Thomas, of Licksville, Frederick county, Md., who was arrested by Officer Volkman, in Georgetown, D. C., about noon yesterday, and who left Washington in the 4:38 p. m. train, failed to reach Frederick county jail. A party of about 75 men, in open daylight and without any disguise, forcibly took him from the custody of Officers Volkman and B. F. Harper, and hung him about 200 yards southeast of the railroad station, at what is known as Sugar-loaf hills.

THE ARREST IN GEORGETOWN.

It was briefly stated in THE STAR of yesterday that he had been apprehended in Georgetown and that he had consented to go to Frederick. Captain Richard Thomas, the husband of the victim of the vile outrage, went to Washington on Wednesday for the purpose of identifying Adam Austin, who had been arrested by Officer Harper on suspicion of being the ravisher. He declared that Austin was not the man, and he was released. Capt. Thomas was confident that Carroll would turn up in Georgetown, where he was well known. Therefore he looked about the canal and aqueduct yesterday. Shortly after 11 o'clock a. m. he saw Carroll near the aqueduct, who put on a bold front and touched his hat to him. Capt. Thomas could scarcely restrain himself and immediately set out to find an officer. He halted Officer Volkman, who was mounted, and pointed out the culprit. Officer Volkman soon got near to him in the vicinity of the aqueduct. Carroll broke into a run and proved himself very swift of foot. He lead the officer and others who joined in the chase for about seven squares in and around the coal docks before he was

RUN DOWN AND SECURED.

He was at once taken to the police station where Capt. Thomas fully identified him. There was found on the prisoner a common, brass-handled clasp knife, such as was described by Mrs. Thomas as the one held to her throat by Carroll while he accomplished his purpose. He admitted knowing Capt. Thomas and tacitly confessed to committing the outrage by stating that he left the neighborhood of Licksville because he knew he would be killed if caught. To your correspondent he said he had just left the farm on which he was engaged because the wages did not suit him; and that he intended to follow boating hereafter, therefore, he had engaged on a boat which arrived in Georgetown Wednesday. Having expressed a willingness to go to Frederick for trial (the offence was committed in that county) it was arranged that Officers Volkman and B. F. Harper should take him there. It was supposed that as the people who gathered at Tuscarora station the evening before were disappointed in not finding the prisoner on the train, there would be no further attempt to lynch him. It was further believed that no notice had been sent up the line of his coming. Anticipating no trouble preparations were made to take him to Frederick.

ON THE TRAIN.

About 3½ o'clock Carroll was brought out of his cell, at the Georgetown station, handcuffed. The officers left Washington with him on the 4:35 western train. Before the departure of the train it was noised about that he was the man who committed the outrage, and large numbers of people pressed into the car to get a look at him. Not a few in his presence made threatening remarks, and expressed the hope that he would not reach Frederick. He manifested a stolid and sulky indifference. The party for Frederick was seated in the rear part of the forward car, Carroll being next the window in the rear seat. Officer Volkman was on his left, and Captain Thomas and Officer B. F. Harper sat opposite. Two representatives of THE STAR were on the train.

CARROLL'S STATEMENT TO A STAR REPORTER.

Carroll talked but little. He said, however, to one of THE STAR reporters that he was about 24 years old, and was born a slave near Smithville, Washington county, Md. His parents were dead, and he had followed boating or working on a farm nearly all his life. For a year past he had worked on a farm near Licksville. He said he was not a church member, and that he used to pray when he was small. Capt. Thomas, however, told THE STAR reporter that Carroll was the leader of a colored prayer meeting and quite an exhorter, but not lately. Knowing something of the excitable character of the people in a case of this kind, THE STAR reporter advised him to say his prayers, and if he had any statement to make in reference to the charge against him to make it. The only answer was a sullen look.

SIGNS OF DANGER TO THE PRISONRR.

When the train reached Barnesville a number of rather rough looking men came aboard and took a look at Carroll. Some of them remarked that that was the damned imp and others went further, in cursing him. They soon left the car. Carroll gave them only a sort of a side look, and scarcely raised his head. By this time there were but few passengers in this car, and not many in the other cars of the train.

THE LYNCHERS' VAN GUARD.

When Tuscarora, four miles south of Barnesville, was reached, six stalwart men entered the car in answer to Capt. Thomas' call through the open door, "I've got him." They took a look at the prisoner and proceeded to the other end of the car, where they seemed to be holding a conference. The officers in charge of the prisoner put on a determined look and braced up, evidently anticipating trouble, but the prisoner, who, besides being handcuffed, had his legs tied closely together, did not seem to realize his danger; and when it was again suggested to him by THE STAR man that as life might be short he had better pray, he paid no more attention than at first.

EXCITED MARYLANDERS BOARD THE TRAIN AND SEIZE THE PRISONER.

The Frederick train at Point of Rocks makes a halt about 200 yards below the station at the foot of Sugar loaf Hill. When the stoppage was made there yesterday the first car was at once besetged by about 75 men. About 15 of them were apparently picked men for the business in hand. Most of them were stalwart canal boat men. The picked fifteen entered the car exclaiming, "Get him out! Get him out!" making a great noise and bustle. The Georgetown officers immediately rose to protest against the seizure of their prisoner. They were themselves seized and held fast by some of the men while others lifted Carroll out bodily. A number remained in the car to prevent the officers going out to interfere.

DRAGGED TO HIS DEATH.

Carroll struggled as best he could to hold to all projections of the car with his hand cuffed wrists. He was lifted to the platform head formost. Just as the lynchers were about to take him off the steps the train from the west came down the other track making it necessary forethem to retain the prisoner on the steps. They held him head downwards.

PREPARING FOR THE EXECUTION.

The lynchers were not idie meantime, and without saying a word produced a rope—a common manilia clothes line about one-half inch in diameter, with a noose in the end. This was placed over the prisoner's head as soon as the western train had passed. Carroll was half carried, half dragged across the now free track to the embankment on the east side of the road. This embankment was six or more feet high, and the mud, a soft yellow clay, rendered it difficult to surmount. Carroll was, however, pulled up by aid of the rope about his neck by those above, aided by others shoving from below. Close to the edge of this bank was a six-rall fence. Over this the doomed man was quickly helped with even less care than was given him when being taken off the train and up the embankment. The party were now in a field of newly ploughed ground, red clay, which was becoming very soft from the drizzling rain that had been falling almost all day. About six men seized the rope and four partially raised Ca

When the rope tightened around his neck and the hauling was resumed, he managed to cry brokenly, "My God, you are killing me." "You of a —, that's what we are after" was the answer. The rest of the distance to a small black walnut sapling was made in a couple of minutes.

A SPEEDY EXECUTION.

No time was lost here. The rope was thrown over a small but strong limb of the sapling by a number of young men who climbed it for that purpose. One man kicked Carroll savagely on the head twice as he lay on his back while the rope was going over the limb. Three men at the end of it soon had him swinging with his feet some nine inches from the ground. He drew his tied feet up once or twice and pressed his handcuffed hands against the sapling. A big canal man reached up and forced the victim's head through his handcuffed hands. He died in ten minutes in that position. In his left hand he still held his old black felt hat tightly clinched, and will hold it until his death grip is loosened. As his feet left the ground the drizzling rain increased to a steady fall. The hanging was not a professional one, the knot, instead of slipping to the back of the neck, catching under the left jaw, throwing the face upwards. The crowd stood excitedly talking over the matter for some ten minutes after the hanging. Some of them broke pieces from the sapling to a limb of which the dead body swung, and others carried off pieces of the clothing (badly torn by the rough handling) from the dangling body as ghastly relics of the execution. In fifteen minutes after Carroll's feet left the ground his body swung alone in the cold rain, the tongue protruding about half an inch.

In this case retribution followed swift and sure. The outrage was committed about 12 o'clock Monday night. Carroll arrived in Georgetown Wednesday, and was arrested about noon yesterday. He left Washington at 4:35, in custody, and arrived at Sugar Loaf Hill at 6:32. At 6:45 his dead body was dangling from the limb of a sapling.

Treasurer Gilfillan to-day dispatched his chief clerk to the office of the District Commissioners to notify the latter that hereafter all warrants drawn upon the Treasury department on account of the District funds must be counter-signed by two of the Commissioners. This has taken the latter by surprise, since for a long time such warrants have been countersigned by Captain Phelps, President, by order of the Board of Commissioners, as was mutually agreed upon by the Treasury officials and the District Commissioners. As all the District Commissioners were not present, word was sent back to the Treasury requesting a suspension of such rule until a conference can be held with First Comptroller Porter, who appears to have originated the new departure.

STREET IMPROVEMENTS.

In yesterday's STAR, under the head of "District Government Affairs," allusion was made to a want of funds to commence street repairs and improvements until after the 1st of July next. Hanging of a Fiend.
A TAX-PAYER.

James Carroll, the negro fiend who perpetrated a most diabolical outrage upon the person of Mrs. Richard Thomas, at Licksville, in Frederick county, while being taken to Frederick jail was taken from the train at Point of Rocks by a band of lynchers and hanged until dead. The particulars, as received, are as follows:

The train upon which the prisoner was placed in custody of policeman H. C. Volkman and B. T. Harper, of Georgetown, left Washington at 4:35 P. M., in charge of Conductor Michael. Telegrams conveying intelligence of the arrest had been sent to Point of Rocks during the afternoon, and long before the arrival of the train at this station a large number of enraged and determined men had assembled from various sections of the counties of Frederick and Montgomery, and Loudoun county, Virginia, and it needed no prophetic soul to foretell their stern purpose. At Tuscarora, four miles from Point of Rocks, nearly thirty desperate men, masked and armed to the teeth, boarded the train, but made no demonstration. On arriving at the Washington Junction the train was immediately be seized by nearly three hundred persons, about one hundred of whom were on horseback. — Twenty or thirty men, with pistols and knives drawn, quickly entered the car in which Carroll was seated, and after overcoming the desperate resistance made by the officers and conductor, took up the prisoner bodily and carried him to the platform, where a slip noose was thrown over his head. He was then hurriedly dragged across a plowed field about 100 yards to the nearest tree. Here the rope was immediately thrown over a limb and instantly grasped by a dozen hands, and almost in the twinkling of an eye the fiend in human form was dangling in the air. Not a word was spoken by him, and he died without a struggle, a victim to his brutish passions and to the terrible vengeance of an enraged and outraged community. The whole affair was proceeded with in a cool and deliberate manner, and was over in less than thirty minutes — After he was pronounced dead the masked horsemen at once mounted their horses and rode quietly away. Several times the policemen from Georgetown attempted to cross the field to where the prisoner had been taken, but pistols placed in close proximity to their heads effectually warned them that they were treading upon dangerous ground. Threats from the maskers were frequently heard to the effect that if the authorities had succeeded in getting the prisoner to the Frederick jail their sworn determination to lynch him could not have been thwarted, for they would certainly have attacked the building. Carroll confessed to the perpetration of the crime before leaving Washington.
Additional details received of the horrible outrage perpetrated by Carroll are even more harrowing than these first reported. After effecting an entrance into the house through a window, Carroll proceeded immediately to the chamber where Mrs Thomas and several children were sleeping. Reaching the bedside he grasped her by the throat, and by threatening to kill her with a knife that he held in his hand, compelled her to desist from her struggles; one of the children began to cry, when he savagely caught it by the hair and threw it roughl aside. The imprint of his fingers could still be seen on Mrs. Thomas' neck the next day. She is reported to be in a prostrate and precarious condition, while her husband is terribly distressed. The people in the vicinity were enraged to such an extent that they were opposed to granting the outrage a trial. Carroll was 22 years of age, dark brown in color, nearly black, rather raised nose, thick lips, weight about 150 pounds, about 5 feet 8 inches high.

THE POINT OF ROCKS LYNCHING.
The lynching of James Carroll colored, at Point of Rocks on Thursday night, for the outrage on Mrs. Richard Thomas, of Licksville, Md., on Monday night last, was the absorbing topic of conversation in Frederick county to-day. The cool and deliberate manner in which the preparations were made for the lynching, and the summary mode in which the prisoner was dealt with, showed a determination on the part of the residents of the county not to wait for the slower verdict of the law, and if the man had succeeded in getting to Frederick City jail there were 500 armed men ready to tear or burn down the building and capture the ravisher.

Mr. Richard Thomas, the husband of the unfortunate lady who was the subject of attack, says that when he was in Georgetown, D. C., on Wednesday, walking along the canal path, he met the negro, who raised his hat to him and said, "Good morning, Mr. Thomas." Mr. Thomas passed on and warned Mr. Hy. C. Volkman, a mounted policeman of the third precinct. After following the man for about seven squares Mr. Volkman became afraid he would lose his man amongst the lumber yards in the neighborhood, and, dismounting, continued the pursuit on foot and captured the fellow.

As heretofore shown the prisoner was taken to the Washington depot of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad and left for Frederick by the 4.30 P. M. train in charge of officers H. C. Volkman and B. F. Harper and in company of Mr. Richard Thomas and his brother, F. C. Thomas. About this time a number of farmers were gathered around the depot at Point of Rocks. Ever since Tuesday last there had been a vigilant search for the criminal. Men left their labor and scoured the country night and day in the hope of capturing the outrager. On Thursday afternoon a telegram was received from Sandy Hook that a colored man answering the description of Carroll had been seen at the caves near that place. While waiting to bear further as to this news the following telegram was received by Messrs. Jarboe and Offut from Mr. F. C. Thomas, "Prisoner caught, will leave on 4.30 train. Send notice to Lickville. Meet Dick at Depot."

As soon as this message was received a hurried consultation was held by those present, and in a few minutes a mounted messenger, bearing the name of "Brick" Pomeroy, although not akin to the Western political economist, started to bear the message to the neighbors in the county. The fiery cross in the times of Rhoderick Dhu and the Scottish clans could not have been carried swifter, and in about an hour from 125 to 150 men, some on foot, others on horseback, and about 25 of them colored, had gathered near the depot. Several of them boarded the train at Tuscarora, four miles from Point of Rocks, but gave no intimation as to the object of their journey. As the train drew near the depot it stopped on the siding in order to allow the east bound train to pass. At this juncture about twelve or fifteen men entered the car in which the prisoner was seated with his captors, and, seizing him, began to drag him to the platform. The police officers protested, but uselessly, and as soon as the man had reached the platform of the car a rope, with an ordinary noose, was placed around his neck, and he was dragged towards the ground. As he fell, with his head on the track and his feet in the air, the east-bound train passed by, narrowly missing the half-strangled man, and almost striking one of the vigilantes, who was holding to him. As soon as the train had passed he was dragged across the track, in the pouring rain, towards a fence at the foot of a steep hill adjoining the track. Over the fence his captors dragged him, shouting, "Up the hill with him?"

At this juncture the rope broke, and a halt was made to refix it. Officer Volkman then appeared on the scene, and called out, "Gentlemen, I appeal to you in the name of the law and of the State of Maryland, let the prisoner go." The answer came back, "Go away from here," and the reply was, "I shall only go by force." Then half a dozen men caught the officer, lifted him bodily over the fence, and placing him in the car kept guard over him. Across the plowed field a hundred willing hands dragged the half-dead negro until they reached a thicket of trees on the brow of the hill. Close to a tall yellow poplar stood a walnut sapling, about twelve feet in height. A youngster jumped up and threw the rope into a forked limb. With a quick jerk the man, who all this time was prostrate, was dragged into the air. Capt. Wilson J. Vance, a native of the largest state in the Union if flattened out—we were on our way to the county in which Capt. Vance first saw the light—Berkeley county, West Va. The route being over the Metropolitan branch of the Baltimore & Ohio railroad, and the train making but few stops, there was but little time to notice the country along the road. It was, however, observed that there were but few, if any, shabby-looking places in view; that farm houses wore an aspect of thrift and good management; that the corn was looking up (after a recent rain), and cabbage heads were assuming a healthy rotundity, and already the ploughman had commenced his preparations for the next season. HARPER'S FERRY AND PIES.

"Here's yer pie," was the sound that greeted the ear, rendering it impossible to hear the brakeman's announcement of Harper's Ferry, the scene of John Brown's exploits. The pie peddlers seemed to monopolize the whole business of the town, and a stranger looking out asked if all Harper's Ferry had gone into the pie business. In a few minutes the now familiar sound, "Here's yer pie," died out in the distance, as the passengers got a glance at John Brown's fort, and in about thirty minutes we were landed at

MARTINSBURG,

"the gate of the Shenandoah Valley." In less than thirty minutes more the writer was installed as a guest at the St. Clair, where he partook of a dinner so good that its effects were observable in the fit of his clothing. At this point the round houses and workshops of the B. & O. R. R. are located, as also the depot of the Cumberland Valley railroad, which, running to Harrisburg, Pa., a distance of 94 miles, gives the people an outlet northward. The population is now about 7,000, and the community is well provided with churches and schools, there being 11 of the former, some of them comparing favorably with churches of more populous and wealthy cities. Rev. George V. Leech, formerly of East Washington M. E. church, is stationed here, having succeeded last week Rev. M. F. B. Rice. There are four commodious school buildings in the town, located judiciously. Judging from the newspapers the people are about equally divided politically, although the "burg" has now a democratic mayor (Mr. Logan), and is the home of the democratic member of Congress from that district, John Blair Hoge.

THE NEWSPAPERS are not at all weakly, although appearing but once a week, but getting their support from the town and surrounding country they are reported as paying their expenses and doing something for those engaged in their conduct. The Statesman, located in the property adjoining Mr. Hoge's residence, is the democratic organ, and is conducted by the Elchelbergers (father and son); the Herald, published by Riley & Golden, is regarded as the republican paper, and the Independent has for its editors and proprietors Messrs. Wisner & Logan, the first named being the postmaster and the manager of the republican side of the paper, Mr. Logan, the democratic mayor, managing the other side. Thus this paper is prepared to cut right and left. To the Elchelbergers and Messrs. Wisner & Logan is the writer indebted for favors, the former having taken him to the highest point in town, the cupola of the St. Clair, whence many interesting points could be seen, such as the magnificent farm of Hon Charles James Faulkner, a couple of miles south, and the extensive Hannis distillery, on the western suburbs of the town. The town is supplied with gas and water, has a steam fire engine, and although the railroad company is working only about half force in the shops there are indications of a revival of trade, for a company has been formed to erect iron works, from which great things are expected.

MARTINSBURG WIDOWS.

The peculiar business of the trip requiring the writer to interview several families in the town as to family matters he ascertained that some Martinsburg girls, by reason of the war, had become widows, some being relics of those who wore the blue, and some of those who wore the gray. After his experience he will say that a more lively set of widows he never met. Being rather an oldish man the girls kept shy of him, and the only opportunity he had of seeing the young lady portion of the town was when having bid Mr. Hamill, of the St. Clair, good-bye and made his way to the depot he beheld some thirty or forty fair Martinsburgers form in line on the railroad platform to take the train for Harper's Ferry to assist there in a church concert.

There was but little talk of politics in and around the "burg," but from the little said it is to be presumed that the republican candidate for Congress will be elected, owing to the fact that the democrats have two candidates, and should the latter not settle on one candidate, the republicans will have, they say, good prospects of victory.

IN COLORADO. The first case of note was at Lake City, Colorado, on the 27th ult. Two men, named Browning and Belts, kept a low drinking and gambling den in the place, and besides had been guilty of various bold acts of burglary. About Wednesday of last week it was found that a burglary had been committed in an unoccupied building in the town where goods had been stored, and as there were still valuable goods in the building, Sheriff Campbell and his assistant, named Smith, took position in the house on Wednesday night to watch for the burglars. About 2 o'clock in the morning a couple of men, with false keyes, entered the house, and striking a match, Campbell, seeing they were Belts and Browning, called to them to throw up their hands. Instead of doing so Belts fired, putting a bullet through the sheriff's heart. Smith returned the fire, but seeing his chief fall remained to assist him while the burglars got away. Early next morning, however, both were caught, and a coroner's jury having been called and placed the guilt of the two men beyond a doubt, they were placed in the city jail with a guard around them. That night, however, 70 masked men took them by force out of the jail, marched them to the Ocean Wave bridge across the Gunnison river, and hanged them. The bodies were guarded until next morning, when the officers of the law cut them down and had them buried.

AT MINNEAPOLIS. On Thursday afternoon of last week a brutal assault was made on a child less than four years old near a school house in the suburbs of Minneapolis, by a ruffian named Frank McManus, subsequently learned to have come there lately from Boston. Several women caught him in the act and were the means of his arrest. The child was so cut and lacerated by the brute that its life is despaired of. The fiend was placed in the county jail, but at night it having been rumored that the child was dead, 70 disguised citizens went to the jail and taking McManus out by force conveyed him to the vicinity of the school house, where they strung him up on the limbs of a stout oak tree. At 8 o'clock next morning his dead body was cut down by the coroner and buried.

At GALION, OHIO. Recently a negro, Frank Fisher, at Galion, Ohio, under circumstances of extreme brutality, committed a rape on a 13-year old German girl of that place named Barbara Kettig, the negro making his escape. The strictest search for him was set on foot at once, resulting in his arrest last Sunday morning at Frederickstown. On being conveyed to Gallon to jail a mob of several thousand people soon surrounded the place determined to lynch him. The officers were powerless against the infuriated crowd. The negro was seized, and marched to the bedside of his victim for identification, and she promptly, on seeing him, answering "That is the man," a noose was thrown over his head and he was dragged to a tree in the rear of the lot. His hands were tied behind his back, a hankerchief put over his face, and he was strung up at 4:10 o'clock P.M. on Sunday. The mob when satisfied that he was dead, quietly dispersed.

Attempt on; the Life of W. H. Vanderbilt and Cyrus W. FIELD,

A dastardly attempt was made last Saturday in New York city, by some miscreant on the lives of Wm. H. Vanderbilt and Cyrus W. Field. About 4 o'clock in the afternoon a couple of paste board boxes, about the size of cigar boxes, were dropped into the post office duly stamped and directed to the individuals named. They were placed in the mail bags and sent to the up-town district by the elevated railway. On the way one of the boxes exploded in the mail bag, setting it on fire, whereupon it was transferred to the platform and then placed on a wogan and taken to the 29th street post office station and opened and contents examined. It was found that the explosion had occurred in the package addressed to Vanderbilt, upon which the other—addressed to Field—was submerged in water and then carefully opened. Inside of it was found a tin box containing about a pound of powder, with a vial, containing sulphuric acid and a white salt, afterwards ascertained to be chlorate of potash, so placed that, on drawing a string, the sulphuric acid and white powder would cause an explosion, of course sufficient to endanger the life of any one holding the box in his hand. Fortunately neither box reaching its destination, both gentlemen escaped. A similar box, on the same evening, was left at the door of Superintendent Walling, of the city police force.

"I don't think the frontier ever witnessed a lynching so bold as that of Betts and Browning," said Mr. Hickman, the Receiver of the Land-office at Lake City, to a Tribune reporter yesterday. "You will remember the cause. Sheriff Campbell attempted to arrest the two men, you know, while they were in the act of stealing some furniture from a house. He was shot and killed instantly—an assistant who was with him identifying the faces of the murderers by the light of a match which was struck when the demand for surrender was made. The murder was committed on the 26th of last month, the day we were to have celebrated the Odd Fellows' anniversary. The Sheriff was the founder of our lodge, and instead of a celebration we had a funeral. A better fellow than Campbell never lived. The murderers were the keepers of a dance-hall. They were arrested that morning and put in jail. Campbell's two brothers, who were mining at Pitkin, eighty-five miles away, were telegraphed to come to Lake City to attend the funeral. That afternoon, the 27th, a rumor was circulated in the streets that there would be a prayer-meeting at the house of the dead Sheriff at eleven o'clock. I had not the slightest suspicion of the intention, and was among the 100 men or more who congregated near the premises. I was not there long before I had learned the purpose of the advertisement, and was not slow in washing my hands of the affair. The men had met to lynch the murderers. The plan was given out boldly, and as boldly executed, as the next day, when I arose, the information I received before I had reached the breakfast table was that the lifeless bodies of the two men were hanging from the cross-beam of the Gunnison River bridge, below the city."

"Did you hear how the vigilantes proceeded?"
"From the gossip which was circulated after the excitement and precaution had died out, I believe that at least 100 men were in the lynching party. I will tell you the occurrence as I framed it from mixed reports. From the 'prayer-meeting' the vigilantes went to the jail. The guards, apparently, offered no resistance, and Betts and Browning were taken out. The hands were first bound to their sides. Some of the representative church-members of the community are said to have been in the throng who demanded the 'eye for an eye and the tooth for a tooth.' I do not know how true that was. Well, while the men were being bound, one of them asked if there was not a friend in the crowd. A young gambler who had been a frequenter of the dance-hall, and a friend of the doomed men, shouted that he was a friend, and made a break toward the prisoners. Somebody placed the cold muzzle of a pistol against the side of his head and told him to skip the town instanter. I believe that the incident was a true bill, because the courageous youth was not seen about the city until a week later. Everything was done quietly, dispassionately. The two men were marched down the Gunnison road after midnight. Neither of them weakened, even when the cruel nooses were placed about their necks. An effort was made to save Browning, many insisting that he did not fire the fatal shot, and should not be lynched for complicity in the murder. Browning would have been turned loose had it not been for the fact that he said he would be revenged upon the witnesses of the murder. When he made this threat he was deemed a better man dead than alive, as everybody knew that, although a quiet man, he was desperate. Just as the hanging bee was being ended, and, I understand it, while the ropes being arranged for the pulling, the two Campbell brothers arrived at the scene, having rode the eighty-five miles by buckboard and in the saddle that day. The murderers were asked if they had aught to say, and both coolly replied that they had not. They were hanged to a beam which crosses above from truss to truss of the bridge. The bodies were allowed to dangle there until late in the day. They were planted, however, before the remains of the Sheriff were interred."

"Was there any indignation expressed against the lynching?"

"Not the least. On the contrary, the people all thought the act a good one, and all that could be heard in the way of comment indicated a feeling of relief and satisfaction.—Denver (Col.) Tribune.

MARYLAND.
A Large Vote-Independents Ahead.
Special Dispatch to THE EVENING STAR:
BALTIMORE, Nov. 7.—The election is very animated, but entirely peaceful. The poll up to one o'clock aggregated forty-five thousand out of a possible total of sixty thousand votes. It is unusually large in its vest pocket character. No estimate but what is entirely conjectural can be made. The indications are favorable to the independent judiciary ticket of three democrats and one republican.

The Congressional vote is closer, with indications favorable to the democratic ticket.

[By Associated Press.]

Three-Fourths of the Vote of Baltimore Polled at Noon.

BALTIMORE, Nov. 7.—The election in this city is progressing very quietly. Up to 12 o'clock to-day, it is estimated that three-fourths of the vote of the city was polled. Since that time it has been showery, and the voting was not so fast. The independent judiciary ticket is polling a heavy vote.

A Colored Man Killed at the Polls in Frederick.

FREDERICK, MD., Nov. 7.—At one of the voting precincts in this city this morning a fight occurred between a number of negroes and whites, during which Israel Groff, a colored man, was shot by a policeman named Augustus Porter and instantly killed.

THE SIXTH MARYLAND. The Contest in Washington County- The District Claimed for McComas (Rep.)-Gov. Hamilton at Work.
Special Dispatch to THE EVENING STAR.

HAGERSTOWN, MD., Nov. 7.—The fight in Washington county between Montgomery Blair and Louis E. McComas is being waged very bitterly. Mr McComas has received information from Allegheny county that A. F. George, the greenback-labor candidate for Congress, has withdrawn and is endeavoring to persuade the workingmen in that county to vote for Blair. Mr. George has sold out, but cannot deliver the goods, as great numbers of workingmen are voting open tickets for McComas. Washington county will give McComas 250 majority. The republican judicial ticket will also pull through. The democrats are making a very desperate effort to carry the county for Blair, but cannot succeed. Gov. Hamilton is working at the polls in district No. 3 with the roughs and shoulder-hitters, endeavoring to save his party from their impending doom in western Maryland.

The Shooting at Frederick.

THREATS OF LYNCHING MADE—A GREAT NUMBER OF FIGHTS.

Special Dispatch to THE EVENING STAR.

FREDERICK, MD., Nov. 7.—The town is all excitement over the shooting of a colored man named Isaac Gross by Officer Porter. There are conflicting opinions as to what was the cause of the affair. A large mob is congregated around the residence of Hon. John A. Lynch, where Porter is in the charge of the sheriff and his deputies, and threats are made of lynching the officer.

There has been a great number of fights, and different parties have been badly hurt. It is hard to form any idea of how the election will go in this county, but the general opinion is Matter, for associate judge, will receive from 800 to 1,000 majority, while McComas, for Congress, will probably receive from 500 to 600.

In an altercation at one of the voting precincts in Frederick, Md., between a number of white and colored men Israel Groff, colored, aged about 28 years, was shot by Policeman Augusta Porter and instantly killed. Porter immediately fled, and took refuge in the residence of Hon. John A. Lynch, judge of the circuit court. A mob of several hundred colored men, highly incensed, gathered about the lawn and demanded his surrender. Appeals for quiet and order were made by Chief Judge Ritchie, Judge Lynch, and others, and the crowd was finally induced to disperse, the prisoner in the meantime having been taken by the sheriff in an indirect way to the jail. The shooting of Groff was nothing less than a deliberate murder.

There was a serious affray between negroes and whites in Wilmington, Del., in which the negroes used pistols freely, and the whites retaliated with a shower of bricks and stones, which scattered their assailants. Two white men, William Barton and Martin Fagan, were seriously wounded by bullets and several hurt by bricks. A woman was also shot in the breast but not seriously injured. Senator Bayard remained at the eleventh ward polls all day. Many arrests were made during the afternoon, among them Chief Engineer McNairre, chairman of the city Democratic committee, for knocking down a man.

The Twenty-sixth ward of Philadelphia gave a Republican gain of 400.

In a row at the polls in Chicago, George A. Kelly, a fireman, was shot and killed by John Flaherty, a special policeman.

Rev. W. C. Campbell has retired from the editorship of the Presbyterian News, at Roanoke, Va., the rapid increase of his congregation, and consequent increase of his labors in that direction, necessitating the step.

On Sunday morning of last week, Rev. J. C. Bowman, who has been pastor of the German Reformed Church at Shepherdstown, for the last seven years, tendered his resignation to the officers of that church, to take effect at an early date. Mr. Bowman has accepted a call from the Reformed congregation at Hanover, Pa.

W. M. Swain, a train hand in the employ of the Shenandoah Valley Rilroad Company, was arrested in Hagerstown Monday night, for shooting at Geo. W. Howe, another train hand. A hearing was held before Justice Brezler, when Swain acknowledged to the shooting, giving as a cause for the deed the fact that he was laboring under the influence of liquor. He gave bail to appear before the grand jury.

The Spirit of Jefferson says: The Union Bee Keepers' Association of Maryland, Virginia and West Virginia met in Hagerstown, Md., Wednesday week. The following officers were elected for the ensuing year: President, D. A. Pike, Smithburg, Md.; vice president, Thos. Tooter, Cumberland, Wm. E. Anderson, Harper's Ferry, E. C. Jordan, Stephenson, Va.; secretary, J. Luther Bowers, Berryville, Va., treasurer, S. Valentine, Hagerstown. Various subjects of importance to the members were discussed.

A riot occurred at Frederick, Tuesday, during the progress of the election, in which Israel Groff, colored, was shot and killed by Augustus Porter, a police officer. A mob of negroes pursued Porter, who took refuge in the residence of Judge Lynch. Threatening demonstrations were made about the dwelling, but at the solicitation of Judge Lynch and others the crowd finally dispersed. It appears that the person who instituted the riot refused arrest, when the officer drew his revolver and shot Groff, another party to the difficulty, it is alleged, through mistake.

The Shepherdstown Register says: Mr. J. Howard Strider, of Duffield's, went to Nokomis, Montgomery Co., Illinois, some time since to visit his parents, whom he had not seen for twenty years, they having moved west to take up their residence. About the middle af September, his son, Mr. N. S. J. Strider, was summoned by telegraph, as his father was very ill. He staid until it was thought Mr. Strider was out of danger, and then returned home. The other day he received news that his father had relapsed and died on Saturday, October 21st. Mr. Strider was well known throughout the county, having been born and raised near Duffields.

a farmer near Huntington, Ind., set her clothing on fire with a candle the other night and was fatally burned.

JAMES E. ANDERSON, editor of the Eureka (Nevada) Leader, died on the 6th from wounds received in a shooting affray with G. F. Reek, a candidate for Superintendent of Public Instruction.

While a passenger train on the St. Joseph & Western road was approaching Alexandria, Neb., the other night, the lower trucks of the tender became detached and the baggage-car was overturned. Frank Hurst, a brakeman, was killed, and Conductor Scott Sharpe was seriously injured.

HENRY C. SEIMKUHLER, a New Orleans fireman, was thrown from his steamer the other day and killed by the wheels of a following truck.

AUGUST WESTFIELD, a young clerk who was to have been married in Baltimore, Md., on the 6th, fell from a Locust Point ferryboat and was drowned. The body was recovered, and by some mistake sent to the house of his intended, where the minister and invited guests had assembled. THIRTY workmen were killed by an explosion in the Clay Cross Mines, in Derbyshire, England, on the 7th.

A FIRE on the water front at Portland, Maine, swept away establishments valued at nearly $250,000.

A NUMBER of men forced their way into the jail at Vienna, La., the other night, and pounced upon four negroes sent there from Jackson Parish, charged with robbery and assault. One of the prisoners made his escape immediately upon reaching the door. He was fired on three or four times without effect. Another was given a chance for his life, as he was thought innocent. The other two were found dead, the next morning, about a mile out of town, their bodies riddled with bullets.

THE late Jerome G. Kidder, of Boston, Mass., left large bequests to a dozen charities, including a sum to be expended in sending destitute strangers to their homes.

EN earthquake shock was experienced in Laramie City, Wyo., on the 7th. It was plainly felt all along the line of the Union Pacific Railway west as far as Evanson. Plastering fell off in the buildings at Rawlins, Point of Rocks and other points.

JOHN N. BEACH, 17 years of age, who is wanted in Chicago for forgery, surrendered himself at the Central police-station in Cincinnati, the other day. His father is a leading wholesale grocer at Minneapolis, Minn.

HENRY HEISEL, a saloon-keeper at West Chester, Ohio, was killed and his wife fatally injured by two burglars the other morning. Messrs. Kelly and Costello, who answer the description of the murderers, have been arrested in Cincinnati.

G. A. KELLY, a Chicago fireman, was killed by John Flaherty, a special policeman, during a disturbance at the polls. A negro named Israel Groff drew a revolver upon Policeman C. A. Porter at a polling-place in Baltimore, Md., and was shot dead before he could use it.

OLIVER's wire-mill, Pittsburgh, Pa., burned on the 7th. The loss was $100,000, and it is fully covered by insurance. Eight hundred men are thrown out of employment. The fire originated through a workman placing a lighted lamp near a barrel of oil, thereby causing an explosion.

F. A. DOUBLEDAY and an unknown man were burned to death in New York City on the 8th. A spark from an electric wire caused the explosion of a quantity of varnish.

PROVIDENCE, Nov. 18.—John Murray, of Cranston, age thirty three, a painter, fell from a staging this afternoon and was fatally injured.

ATLANTA, Ga., Nov. 18.—A. N. Neal, a white man, was arrested at Conye's yesterday and placed in jail on a charge of assulting his wife's niece, a girl ten years of age.

EASTON, Penn., Nov. 18.—Mrs. Mary Nolf, of Phillipsburg, N. J., attempted to commit suicide last night by taking laudanum, on account of a difficulty with her husband, she is still alive.

SUICIDE AT THE AGE OF NINETEEN.
WASHINGTON, Nov. 18.—Miss Amelia Kahler, a handsome woman, age nineteen, living at No. 1,762 K-st., took the case of a poison yesterday. She died from the effects of the poison this evening.

INTURED BY A TOY PISTOL.
SHENANDGAH, Penn., Nov. 18.—While Joseph Boyer, age thirteen, was playing to-day with a toy pistol, in which there was a blank cartridge, 22-calibre, the pistol was accidentally discharged and a hole two inches square was torn in his hands. It is said the merchant who sold the pistol will be prosecuted.

TWO NEGROES SENTENCED FOR MURDER.
GOLDSBORO, N. C., Nov. 18.—The trial of Robert Pratt and Francis Moore, negroes, for the killing of O'Neal, a white man, closed here today. Pratt was sentenced to be hanged on January 19, and Moore to twenty years' in the penitentiary. There were five negroes on the jury. Moore, when sentenced, confessed the crime.

A POLICEMAN RELEASED ON BAIL.
FREDERICK, m.d., Nov. 18.—Policeman Porter, who shot John Israel Moore, colored, on the day of election, was ad; matted to bail to-day by Judge Lynch. It was feared that there might be some riotous demonstration when Porter was brought to the Court House, but everything passed off very quietly.

TO BE BE TRIED FOR ROBBING CARS.
NORTH ADAMS, Mass. Nov. 18.—Lester Howard, an employee of the Troy and Greenfield Railroad Company, who is charged with robbing freight cars, had a hearing to-day and was sent to jail for trial. The Great Poker Game.

NEWYORK, June 15th.—A special to the Times from Newburg, N. Y., of June 13th thus describes the great poker game in which Dr. Montreville M. Hedges and William M. Scott are accused of having swindled Francis P. Weed out of $150,000 by means of stocked cards: This remarkable game, according to the papers in the case, was played one evening last June in Dr. Hedges' dental rooms, on the corner of Water and Second streets, in this city. When the party was seated Dr. Hedges secured the deal, and delivered five cards to each player. The Doctor dealt himself a full hand, Scott obtained a four flush and Weed received three aces. Scott called for one card and secured a straight flush. Weed took two cards, one of which was an ace, making his hand four aces. Dr. Hedges' hand was what is known as a "pat," and he played it without drawing. Weed's first bet on his four aces was, it is said, $1,000, which his opponents both saw and raised him $1,000 each. The play continued with raises of $1,000 until the betting on each hand had reached $10,000 or $15,000, when Weed hesitated and said: "Look here, boys, how are you going to pay this thing if I get it?" Scott and Hedges satisfied him of their ability to make good any losses they might sustain, and the play continued till the sum of $150,000 was pending on each hand, the pot having swelled to the immense amount of $450,000. A call was then made, and Scott with his straight flush raked the table, Weed and Hedges being the losers. Whether Hedges made any apparent settlement or not, has not yet appeared, but Weed, it is said, compromised his debt of honor a few days after for $120,000. Standing in the stone corridor of the Charlottesville jail this morning and looking down at a white pine coffin, at the head of which a little stream of blood issued, making a pool on the stone floor. I saw what is probably the last scene in one of the most thoroughly brutal tragedies that have marked the history of Virginia. In the pine box lay Jim Rhodes the murderer, his neck scarred by the rope, and his wrists bruised by the tightness with which they had been bound eight hours before. In a cell above me sat his brother, Leroy Rhodes, deathly white and in an agony of terror; for but for the intercession of the kind-hearted jailor the night before, he too would have been a corpse.

THE MURDER OF MR. AND MRS. MASSEY.

There is a section of Albemarle county called the "Flat Woods." You strike it just after crossing Montcello mountain. It is for the most part inhabited by a class of whites who combine every bad quality, ignorance, vice and violence—a district which the better class of the county have mentally marked as "dangerous." Near the edge of this desert lived John O. Massey and his wife, both nearly seventy years of age. He was a thrifty, industrious farmer, who in a long and excellent life, was supposed to have saved up considerable money. His face was familiar at the county town but not at the county bank, and he was believed to keep his savings at home. It was this that cost the old couple their lives. No one lived in the house with them but a little five year old colored girl. Mrs. Massey was his second wife to whom he had been married about three years.

In the month of March, last, James Clarke Rhodes, who had been absent from his home some four years—serving a term in the Tennessee penitentiary, escaped from that prison and returned to his home in the "Flat Woods." On the night of Wednesday, the 7th of that month, he murdered the Masseys. The door of the chamber of the old people opened into the passage, and the door of a flight of stairs leading down into the cellar of the house, also opened into the same passage. Rhodes went to the house soon after dark, and before the old people had retired, and entering the kitchen where the little girl slept, through a window, went down into the cellar and came up the steps which opened into the passage. The old people came out from their chamber to see what was the matter, the old man carrying an old-time, disused gun, and the aged wife following with a lamp, when Rhodes murdered Mr. Massey first with the axe, and then the wife. When found next morning Mr. Massey was lying on his back, feet to the back door; head to the front; no shoes on; left hand clinched, small abrasion on the little finger, received as though warding off a blow; gash one and one-half inches on left cheek, in line of the mouth; hole in left temple; deep gash from line of the eye-brows, extending down the nose, crushing in the frontal bone to the brain, severing all connection with brow and face. The latter blow supposed to have been deliberately struck when Mr. Massey was down and almost dead, and which of itself would have caused immediate death. There were five blows from the axe on his head; the race swollen and unrecognizable. Mrs. Massey was found three feet from her husband, her limbs drawn up and her tongue between her teeth, as though she died in great agony. She was as thoroughly saturated with blood as though she had been dipped in a tank of it. Her right temple was mashed into the brain; another blow of the same coaracter on the back of the head, and a large bruise on the spinal column.

The discovery of one awrul murder was made the next morning by the colored man, whose habit it was to come at daybreak and make the fires for the old peole. The little colored girl was too young to tell anything, except that she hid behind the door during what she thought was a fight. MISTAKEN FOR A MURDERER AND THREATENED BY A MOB AFTER HIS DISCHARGE.

FULTON, N. Y., January 1.—In 1805 a man named Simpson was murdered in Richmond, Ky., by his nephew, named Rogers, who lived in the neighborhood. Rogers escaped, and descriptions of him were sent all over the country. In June last Patrick Simpson, of this village, who went away four years ago, was arrested in Columbus, O., on a charge of being the murderer. The arrest was made on the ground of his resemblance to the pictures and description of Rogers, and it was claimed that he had assumed the murder man's name to aid him in escaping detection. Acquaintances of Rogers came from Richmond and positively identified Simpson as Rogers, and he was taken to Richmond on a requisition from the Governor of Kentucky. A mob of moonshiners, awaiting his arrival, attempted to lynch him, but were prevented. The jail guard was doubled and he was saved from the mob. Three times he was committed on habeas corpus proceedings.—In October, however, he succeeded in showing that he was in Fulton when the crime was committed. The court-house was surrounded by a crowd dissatisfied with the decision of the court. His counsel hurried him into a side-building, and giving him $7, told him to fly from the country or he would lose his life.—Simpson secreted himself till night, then swam the Kentucky river, and reached the mountains. Threading the thickets during the night and lying concealed in the daytime, he put hundreds of miles between himself and Richmond before he dared to travel openly. He has just reached home, worn out with anxiety and suffering.

—The uniformity of toilet which has now become the fashion in London and Paris owes its origin to the Queen of Italy. At a special ball got up for her on her recent visit to Vienna, the young beauties of that graceful capital all wore white in her honor, and she herself was draped entirely in white satin, trimmed with silver gauze, looped with gardenias, and set off by strings of the seed pearl, which is the latest fashionable revival. The white Austrian uniform, too, chimed in appropriately. So in remembrance of the compliment Queen Marguerite, at the first ball on her return, made it known that her fair guests were to imitate the beauties of the Austrian capital. And so at the latest tails in London and Paris the "uniform toilet" is the rage, and ladies are expected to appear in some stated tint.

—The Princess of Wales was once almost as tasteless in dress as her mother-in-law. Even yet her example of screening a neck of rather lengthy proportions has given a ridiculous habit of muffling in England to many of the short and most apoplectic dames. But the visits of this charming lady to Paris have gradually developed a genuine fine taste, and the Princess of Wales is fast becoming as much of a sovereign dictator in dress as Eugenie was. When last in Paris she appeared almost always in black. It is the fashionable color of the moment, and, with the quantity of lace worn, transforms Parisian ladies almost into Castilian dames of the sixteenth century, when Spain was under the severe influence of the gloomy Philip II. The Princess usually wears pearls and cat's-eyes, which the superstitious suppose bring good luck.

DENTON, June 5.—About half-past 12 o'clock this morning four masked men, having obstructed the track on the north-bound Missouri Pacific railroad, about a mile and a half north of the depot, attempted to board the express car, but were greeted with a load of buckshot from a gun in the hands of Brownell, the messenger, who followed up his success by firing as they went over the embankment. FRANKLIN, June 5.—To-day the dead body of a man was found lying in the woods near this place. Upon examination it proved to be that of Charles Travers, of Spartansburg, Crawford county, who claimed to be a United States detective, and who has been in the city several days. Two bullet holes were found in his left breast, and by his side a Smith & Wesson revolver with two empty chambers. On his person were found a number of letters, in one of which he declared his intention to destroy himself. Another gave directions as to how his property was to be disposed of and to whom to telegraph to when his body was found, and a third was directed to Miss Mary Whitting, of Cochranton, to whom he was to be married last Thursday, for which event the wedding supper had been prepared, guests and minister had assembled, but Travers failed to come and was not heard of till the body was found to-day. It is undoubtedly a case of suicide.
