OMAHA, August 17th.—The Sioux nation have notified the authorities of a threatened outbreak. This morning Dr. McGillicuddy, Agent of the Red Cloud Indians at Pine Ridge Agency, telegraphed to the Secretary of the Interior, and the dispatch was repeated to the military headquarters in Omaha, stating that he had been informed that Red Cloud and other chiefs of the Sioux at Pine Ridge Agency had come to inform him that unless he was relieved as Agent by October 1st they would break out, and that they had sent word to the post and department commanders to that effect. This afternoon another telegram was received at military headquarters from Major Sumner, of the Fifth Cavalry, commanding at Fort Robinson, stating that he had received a letter signed by fifty-two chiefs of the Sioux nation, saying that widespread dissatisfaction and trouble existed among the bands at Pine Ridge Agency, and they called on General Crook to come up and adjust matters for them. They also said that they had informed the Secretary of the Interior that unless within sixty days Dr. McGillicuddy, their Agent, was relieved and their grievances made right, serious trouble could be expected. The situation is regarded as quite serious by military officers in Omaha who have fought these Indians and know them well. There are about 7,500 Sioux at Pine Ridge, and eighty miles from them, at the Spotted Tail or Rosebud Agency, there are 8,500 under Spotted Tail, Junior, and White Thunder, and to the west one hundred miles 2,500 Crows, who have left their Agency and will not stay on the reservation. They have been killing considerable cattle belonging to ranchmen who have occupied the northern territory with their herds, but no serious trouble has occurred with the Crows. There are also large numbers of Cheyennes among the Sioux, and also a great many warriors returning from Sitting Bull's band, and who used to live with Red Cloud up to 1876, when they struck out with Sitting Bull. They are an element of disturbance. Since the war of 1876 a great many young Sioux have grown up to be warriors, and having listened to the tales of their fathers, they are now anxious to distinguish themselves on the warpath, and are therefore restless and eager for war. It is estimated that the Sioux and their allies can muster over 4,000 warriors, well-mounted and splendidly equipped with arms and ammunition. These Indians, although in the Department of Dakota, a short distance north of the Nebraska line, and under the military supervision of General Terry,

the Department of Arizona, but it is likely that, under the circumstances, he will be specially commissioned to visit these Indians in the Department of Dakota, and listen to their complaints and suggest some remedy. At present he is at Baltimore, but will return to Omaha August 231. What the Sioux grievances are is not definitely known here. Dr. McGillicuddy, the Pine Ridge Agent, bears the reputation of being one of the best agents in the Indian service; is a man of the highest character, with spendid executive ability and wide-spread experience. He served for a number of years as Surveyor in the Engineer Corps on the frontier, and afterwards was Acting Assistant Surgeon in the army. He accompanied all of General Crook's expedition against the Sioux and Cheyennes, and became well acquainted with many of the chiefs. His appointment as Indian Agent was strongly recommended by some of the most prominent military officers, among whom was General Crook. McGillicuddy, who is a man of good judgment and great personal bravery, has many military friends here and elsewhere, who believe that any trouble at the Pine Ridge Agency is due rather to the methods of his department than to any personal incompetency or lack of judgment on his part in fulfilling his duties. His administration has been to carry out the policy of the Government, and it is believed that the Government will sustain him. He was deposed from the Government chieftainship of his people by General Crook in 1876, and Spotted Tall was made chief of all the Sioux. LABORERS' WAR
Between the White and Colored Men on the Memphis and Kansas City Roads.
LITTLE ROCK, August 17.—Trouble for some time has existed between the white and colored laborers on the line of the Memphis and Kansas City railroad in Craighead county. Yesterday the following dispatch was received by Newman Erb, the company's attorney, from Bethune, Smith & Co., contractors, dated Nettleton Station: "To-day parties under the guise of kuklux forced our n-gro help to leave, under penalty of death. We can't do our work unless protected. Can you induce the governor to aid us and the men?" Mr. Erb immediately called upon Governor Churchill, and while holding an interview with him received the following telegram from the president of the company: "Bethune & Smith telegraph that armed men have made their negro laborers quit work under threat of killing them. Will you see at once if protection cannot be given so that the negro force may be kept at work "G. H. NETTLETON, President."

The governor immediately wired the sheriff of Craighead county at Jonesboro, three miles from Nettleton, as follows:

LITTLE ROCK, August 17, 1882.

To Wm. T. Love, Sheriff of Craighead County:

The negro workmen near the town of Nettleton, employed by Bethune & Smith, contractors of the Springfield and Memphis railroad, have been driven off by parties of armed men. Investigate the matter and protect the workmen.

T. J. CHURCHILL,
Governor of Arkansas.

Nothing later has been received to-night.

Macon, April 17.—The writer has noted and treasured up with peculiar pride and interest, the numerous testimonials, tributes and panegyrics which have emanated from every section of the Union in behalf of the blameless career, signal services and distinguished reputation of the deceased senior in the editorial conduct of the Morning News.

It seems late in the day for him to essay to add his "brick" to the fast-growing monumental pile which the literary world is erecting to the memory of the author of "Major Jones' Courtship." But, from his quasi retirement as an active journalist, it was meet and proper that he should stand aside until the brethren in full harness had duly spoken. Now, however, that there is a lull in the requiem dirges which have been sounding from an hundred presses in honor of the departed, modestly, and in your own columns, he would drop his floral offering upon the dead editor.

For forty years the writer had personally known and "read after" him in the charming issues of the Madison Miscellany, whose columns he illustrated with the flashes of his abounding wit and humor, and afterwards as the originator and able conductor of the Savannah Morning News. Later still, he was thrown for sixteen years into closer contact and association with him in the journalistic field.

In all that period we found much to admire in the career of Colonel Thompson, and little—very little—to reprehend. Indeed there was a wonderful equilibrium and uniformity in his writings, albeit always strong and to the point, and more than any other contemporary did he preserve the juste million in the discussion even of the most exciting topics. Yet, when occasion offered or unjustly assailed, no man was quicker to defend himself and even carry the war into Africa. It mattered not whether his antagonist was a United States Senator or occupied any other exalted position; when the gauntlet was thrown down it was promptly taken up, and in every instance he showed himself either conqueror or "worthy of his foeman's steel." But withal, it must be conceded that calmness and moderation were leading qualities in all of his editorials.

As a party man, none stood truer to his colors, while ever ready to point out mistakes and sound a note of warning when needed to his political associates. In short, the course of Col. Thompson was transparently candid and fair upon all subjects, political or otherwise, and hence the recognized fact that the Morning News for integrity of purpose, consistency,
Col. Thompson was transparently candid and fair upon all subjects, political or otherwise, and hence the recognized fact that the Morning News for integrity of purpose, consistency, and conservatism, duly tempered by the progressive spirit of the times, is second to no Southern journal, while in Georgia it is justly regarded as the great balance wheel of public opinion.

The private character of Col. Thompson also was without spot or blemish. Frank and genial in his manners; of a social, communicative spirit; excellent company and always outspoken, he nevertheless sedulously avoided personalities and constantly made friends. Like a ripe shock of wheat he has at length been garnered into the storehouse of the Creator he served so well, and we can only exclaim, "peace to his ashes."

Col. Avery's "History of Georgia," that spicy and timely publication, though treating only in part of one of the most momentous epochs in the annals of Georgia, yet, so far as the field has been covered, exhibits great perspicuity, impartiality and truthfulness. Much of the narrative, while of a personal nature, and largely embracing the career and achievements of the most salient actors in those stirring times, still renders even-handed justice to each, and will bear the test of the most rigid scrutiny. To the author, too, is due the honor of showing in unmistakable characters the important part which Georgia sustained in the drama of the "lost cause." She was then, as now, the pivotal and foremost State of the South, and the weight of her sword was not even second in the struggle to that of old Virginia, the mother of Presidents. Col. Avery, at great pains and industry, has collected and formulated an immense mass of statistical information in his work, which will prove invaluable to the future historian. Himself an important factor in the bloody events of that memorable period, one can but admire the modesty and fairness of the author, and be speak for his effort the success it so eminently deserves.

From the numerous attacks against Gov. Colquitt, which, emanating from his enemies in Atlanta, go the rounds of the State, one would conjecture that our noble Executive was a very Cataline for conspiracy and a Caesar in his ambition. Yet not one of these innuendoes have been substantiated, and it must be consoling to His Excellency to know that in virulence and extravagance they fall far short of the cannards of the last Gubernatorial campaign, when he was so overwhelmingly vindicated by the people at the ballot box. The writer has not even seen Governor Colquitt for six months, and what he writes is simply from the standpoint of justice.

That his refusal to call an extra session of the Legislature was not prompted by personal motives is shown by his positive refusal to allow the use of his name for Congressman at large. That act has received the cordial sanction of three-fourths of the impecunious tax payers of Georgia.

As to the charge that the Governor is caballing for Mr. Hill's place, it can only be said that as yet there is no vacancy, and all unite in the hope that the eloquent Senator will continue to remain in his seat, a faithful sentinel over the interests of the commonwealth, and its able champion.

If, however, in the course of events a vacancy in the Upper House should occur, and the Governor were desirous of filling it, no cabal would be requisite in the premises. In all probability he would be the spontaneous choice of the people, and prove, as hitherto, invincible. Assuredly Georgia could not send a more illustrious and deserving citizen to represent her in the councils of the nation. And this is said with due deference to other bright and shining lights who would nobly represent her in the Senate. The writer, as an "organized Democrat" of the straightest sect, will always support the nominee. But we are not advised that the Governor desires any office, and only trust that he may be allowed to retire in peace without having cause to reiterate the complaint that "republics are always ungrateful."

Evidence That He Was Killed by His Brother-The Charge Against the Negroes Modified.
AUGUSTA, GA, May 9.—As a result of a statement made by a student who was present at the killing of young Rountree, a University student at Athens, Ga., a medical commission exhumed the body, made a post mortem examination, and ascertained that the ball which killed Walter Rountree was of large size and fired from a central fire cartridge, of the kind belonging to the pistol in the hands of young Rountree's brother, while the ball from the negro's pistol was of an entirely different calibre. When the Galveston News reached here at noon yesterday containing a dispatch from Navasota to the effect that Alf Gee had escaped from the sheriff at Washington many said, "I told you so." From a gentleman who came to this city from Washington yesterday the BANNER learns the following particulars in regard to the escape. Gee was arrested Sunday evening and kept under close guard until Tuesday about 10 or 11 o'clock, when he was turned over to the custody of J. H. Hutchinson sheriff of this county. Mr. Hutchinson it appears paroled Gee, who walked about town by himself, going into several stores and talking to different persons. Between one and half past one o'clock Hutchinson left Gee in company with his attorneys in a vacant room over Dr. F. H. Smith's drug store for the purpose of holding a private consultation prior to the preliminary examination which was set for one o'clock at the magistrates office in another building. The consultation over, the attorneys came down stairs and told H. to go up and get Gee and take him to the courthouse as it was time for the trial to commence. Hutchinson replied, "Gee is all right," but remained in the store without going up stairs. In the meantime the justice and prosecuting attorneys came to the store and told H. to hurry up as they were waiting. It is said that the stairway is inside of the store, which had a front and back door. Gee was seen to come down stairs and go out the back way, but this fact attracted no attention as Gee had been allowed to walk about town by himself; when out, Gee was seen to mount Alexander's horse, which was hitched near by, and ride rapidly in the direction of Hardin White's house, where he boarded; this did not create any alarm either, as it was supposed that he was going after papers or something connected with his trial. He failed to return and after the lapse of fifteen or twenty minutes the people made up their minds that he had escaped, and they were correct; he was gone. The greatest indignation was expressed at sheriff Hutchinson who was called vile names and personally assaulted; he was openly charged by the crowd, which numbered between 125 and 150 men, with having turned Gee loose. Hutchinson mounted a freedman's horse, ostensibly to pursue Gee, but our informant says he was next heard of at Courtney, where he took the train south to Hempstead. Gee rode out of town in an southerly direction toward Mullens' bottom field. A considerable portion of the crowd mounted their horses and started in pursuit of Gee, but after getting a little distance out of town some one suggested that part of them go back to town and capture the sheriff, but when they got back the sheriff was not to be found. A young man of Washington states that while Gee was at liberty on the streets a citizen of that vicinity was seen to give him a pistol. When our informant left Washington papers were being prepared and a petition was being gotten up asking the removal of Hutchinson. Mr. Moeller, the brother of the gentleman who was killed, expressed his intention of prosecuting the sheriff, avowing his belief that he willfully allowed the prisoner to escape. The BANNER has no comments to make, the public can form its own conclusions. Wife Murder and Attempted Suicide.

Chico, June 24th.—A most fendish and brutal murder was perpetrated here about 9 o'clock to night. Herr Smidt and as wife came here from Stockton about four weeks ago, and opened a saloon on Main street, called the "Opera." BODY OF THE MISSING MAN FOUND.

STOCKTON, June 25th.—On Thursday night last William Devoll, a well-known citizen of this place, disappeared mysteriously. Not much anxiety was felt until yesterday, when it was ascertained that he was last seen at the tannery near McCloud's lake. This morning several persons commenced dragging the lake near the shore, and he was found at half-past 9 o'clock floating face up twenty feet from the shore, opposite Judge Creanor's place. OROVILLE, June 24th.—Frank Wagner, an old resident of Butte county, died suddenly yesterday at his home at Mount Spring House. Disastrous Fire at Berkeley—The Olive Branch Hotel Burned.

OAKLAND, July 6th.—One of the most disastrous fires ever known in Berkeley occurred early this morning. The large hotel known as the "Olive Branch," situated on Choate street, at the terminus of the Oakland dummy railroad, was totally destroyed. The fire was discovered about 3 o'clock by some of the members of the Mackin family, living directly opposite on Choate street. The entire upper portion of the building was then in flames, and it was evident that it was doomed to destruction. The neighborhood was quickly aroused and a dozen or two men soon gathered and did all that was possible to prevent the spread of the flames. The building containing the Postoffice, Dr. Merrill's drug store and the Chinese school-room are within twenty feet of the hotel, and it was thought at one time that these, too, would be destroyed. It was only by persevering efforts that they were saved. The fire burned fiercely, and by 7 o'clock this morning the hotel was in ruins. The building and furniture were valued at about $5,000, and were partially insured, but the exact amount is not known. Mr. Jackson, the lessee, estimates his loss at $2,500. He has $1,800 insurance, but owing to a delinquency in paying the premium he is fearful that it will not be of any benefit to him.

He was digging around the bowler, in order to get it out of the way, when it suddenly rolled from its place and pinned him against a large sawlog. He was afterwards found by some of his fellow-workmen, who, with the aid of crowbars moved the bowler to one side and extricated the unfortunate man. Deceased was 31 years of age, a native of Maine, and unmarried. He will be buried by the Masons.

The Annual Cornish Wrestling Match.

GRASS VALLEY, July 6th.—The annual Cornish wrestling match at this place was concluded this evening. The prizes were as follows: First, $100; second, $70; third, $50; fourth, $30; fifth, $20; sixth, $10. The meeting lasted two days, resulting in James Pascoe, of Bodie, taking the first prize; Charles Kelly, of Grass Valley, the second; Edward Hoskin, of Nevada City, the third; James Rodda, of Nevada City, the fourth; Samuel Rodda, of Nevada City, the sixth. The matches were witnessed by large crowds on both days.

Killed by Lightning.

SUSANVILLE, July 6th.—Near Buntingville Monday, during a heavy thunder-shower, William Leith, Jr., was struck by lightning and instantly killed.

MARSVILLE, July 6th.—L. N. Breed, D. Fairfield and R. E. Ross were to-day appointed delegates to the Republican State Convention.

Sentenced to be Hanged—Remarkably

Rapid Judicial Proceedings.
OROVILLE, July 6th.—The Chico wife murderer Schmidt was to day sentenced by Judge Hundley to be hanged. The promptness of action displayed in this case is in remarkable contrast to the usual procedure of our Courts in the disposition of criminal cases. The murder was committed on Saturday night, June 24th. He was examined on Wednesday following. On Thursday an information was filed in the Superior Court, and the defendant was arraigned, had able counsel assigned him by the Court, pleaded not guilty, and on Saturday, July 1st, he was tried and found guilty of murder in the first degree—all in less than a week from the commission of the deed—and to-day he has received the sentence of death. He displayed but little feeling or emotion when the sentence was pronounced.

SAN JOSE, July 6th.—D. Sullivan, a native of Ireland, aged 30 years, fell dead from heart disease at Aguirre's ranch, in the Santa Clara hills, Tuesday.

BLAINE AND BELMONT.

WASHINGTON, D.C.. April 27. — Blaine's testimony before the House Committee on Foreign Affairs to-day was of no special interest in itself, as the time was almost entirely taken up in quarreling with Belmont. Blaine accused Belmont of misquoting him. An angry dispute ensued, both men rising and pounding the table with their fists. Some say a fight will follow but that is generally disbelieved.

THE PRESIDENT ADVISES REPRESSION IN ARIZONA.

The message sent Congress by the President calls attention to the necessity of prompt repressive measures in regard to the Cow-boy disturbances in Arizona which have gained such headway as to require a resort to extraordinary remedies in view of the inability of the civil authorities to restore order. The President suggests the use of a part of the army as a posse comitatus, and recommends the passage of an enabling measure with this end in view.

CONGRESS ON THE APACHE.

WASHINGTON, D. C., April 28. — The House resolution was adopted reciting the resent Apache outbreak in Arizona, and calling on the Secretary of War for information as to the number of United States soldiers now in the Territory, and whether the military force now stationed there is sufficient to grant full protection to the people, and also whether any legislation is necessary for the prompt and efficient security of the people against the destruction of life and property by hostile Indians.

THE CHINESE BILL.

In the Senate the Political Disability bill went over, and the Chinese bill was resumed, the question being upon concurring in the amendment striking out the Fifteenth Section which construes "Chinese laborers" to mean both "skilled and unskilled."

After Morgan and Call had finished speaking on the Chinese bill Pendleton maintained that it is the duty of Congress to put its interpretation of the word "laborers" in this bill, not only as a guidance for the officers who have to execute, also in the interest of the Chinese and all parties concerned. Edmunds remarked that ultimately the Chinese would have to decide the question and it would be just as difficult to determine the meaning of the words skilled and unskilled as of the word laborers. Pendleton reiterated his argument and then proceeded to speak in favor of the bill on general ground.

The Star route cases have been resumed and Woodward's testimony continued.

Collision at Sea.

SANDY HOOK, N. Y., April 28.—The steamship Nankin, from New York for Liverpool, was run into by the steamer Clyde this morning and lies in a sinking condition. The passengers were saved. The Clyde is badly damaged forwards.

A Ravisher Lynched.

ST. PAUL, Minn., April 28.—At an early hour this morning a party of masked men took Frank Warner, a trampaged 26 years, from jail, and lynched him. Warner was arrested on a charge of ravishing and brutally mutilating a little four year old girl. Before being hung he confessed the crime.

Hanged by a Mob.

FAIRVIEW, Ky., April 28.—At a logrolling here last Saturday, in a row, Bradford Courts, a young rough, killed James Smith and escaped. A posse of citizens followed him to Courts's house, where they found a large quantity of stolen goods. Courts and his brother William, who was also in the row, were taken to jail at Brookville. Last night a mob took them out and hung them.

Robbers Caught.

LITTLE ROCK, April 28.—A Dallas special gives the particulars of the capture of the men who robbed the Texas Pacific train at Ranger station. The robbers were tracked by blood hounds into a canon near the Brazos river. A hot fight ensued, in which one of the robbers was killed, when his two companions surrendered. More of the robbers are at large with the Rangers in pursuit.

A Reception.

FORTRESS MONROE, April 28th.—The President and Cabinet had a brilliant reception here to-day by the sea and land forces. The North-German School ship Louise, from Havana, participated.

Resolutions were adopted denouncing President Arthur for vetoing the Chinese bill, and characterizing his reasons for doing so as hypocritical.

STANISLAUS METAS, aged nine, arrived at Safford, Arizona, from Stevens' sheep camp with the following dreadful story of the recent Indian massacre: "Before daylight the Indians attacked the camp while we were all asleep. My father and five other men attempted to get their guns, but were too late. The Indians rushed in from all sides and overpowered them before a shot could be fired." The work of slaughter then began. An Indian put the muzzle of his gun against the head of one man and fired, blowing his brains against the door and walls. I saw them kill my mother and two brothers by beating their brains out with stones. They killed five persons, and tied my father and tortured him most dreadfully. He begged them to spare him, but they only tortured him the more, and finally they split his skull with an ax. An Indian squaw, the wife of one of four friendly Apache sheep herders who worked with us, saved my life by holding me behind her and begging them to spare me. When all the Mexicans were dead except me the Indians left." The squaw who arrived with the boy said there were ninety-three Indians in the attacking party. The outbreak is the most disastrous which ever occurred in Arizona, not less than forty persons having been killed.

The town of Galeyville, in Arizona, just over the New Mexico line, has been burned and completely destroyed by Apache Indians. Thirty white people were killed.

While a freight train was crossing a creek near Carbon Hill, Ohio, a trestle gave way, dropping the engine into the water. The engineer and fireman—father and son—were instantly killed, and the head brakeman received fatal injuries.

At Yanceyville, N.C., Postmaster Felix Roan shot and killed Nathaniel Johnston, mortally wounded George Williamson, Jr., and was himself shot in the leg by the latter. Lynchings are occurring with alarming frequency. A few months ago Illinois, Wisconsin and Michigan joined the border states and the territories in substituting mob violence for the action of the courts. A few weeks ago there was a lynching in Indiana which was attended by such adjuncts of a legal execution as a clergyman and a surgeon. Wednesday night two men were lynched together in Kentucky, two together in one town in Colorado, and one in another, and at an early hour yesterday morning a man was lynched in Minneapolis. In all these cases but one there is little or no doubt about the guilt of the victims, but in one case a man was lynched on suspicion, and in Indiana only a week ago a man was hanged by a mob after he had been tried by a jury and acquitted. These violent and lawless proceedings raise once more the question, Is civilization a failure?

It is no justification of a murder by a mob that the victim deserves hanging. The only case of these recent cases in which there is any approach to justification is that occurred in Minneapolis. There the mob killed a man who had committed as atrocious a crime as can be conceived of, but one for which it was not at all likely that he could be legally hanged. In all the other cases the penalty of the law was sufficient. The worst case of all was the one in Indiana, where a mob murdered a man who had been tried and found innocent by a jury. To justify or in any degree excuse that act would be equivalent to the obliteration of all criminal courts and procedure, and the return to the methods of savages. The man may have been guilty, in spite of the verdict, but if verdicts are to be disregarded, and if people are to hang every man whom they think a scoundrel merely because they think so, and without regard to legal evidence, then there is an end to organized society, and to the security of life and property, and social chaos and barbarism are already introduced. Civilization involves something more than the punishment of criminals; criminals are punished by Indians and Hottentots. It involves the ascertainment of guilt by rules of evidence, the execution of the penalties of the law by authorized persons, and the settlement of disputes between man and man, and between society and the individual, by duly-organized courts.

Social order rests on the assumption that law is supreme. But law ceases to be supreme where it is overridden by a mob. The first duty of government is to maintain the law and suppress mob murder, cost what it may.

That one lynching leads to another is undoubtedly true. There is a contagion in lawlessness. The fact that a hundred men can vent their rage against an evil-doer with impunity incites a hundred men in another locality to do the same thing. These frequent lynchings in comparatively old and established communities, where all the instrumentalities for the legal punishment of crime exist, are not sporadic outbreaks of inflamed public sentiment. They are the symptoms of an epidemic. They beget contempt for the courts and a spirit of defiance to the law. Unthinking persons may rejoice in them because they promptly punish scoundrels, but they do more than that; they create a sentiment regarding law and order and the regular tribunals that no community can afford to have created.

George Hester and George Washington, charged with burning a store in DeSoto last week, have been released for lack of evidence.

Three negroes are in jail at Rome, charged with hog stealing.

The residence of Mrs. Whitehead, at Liberty Hall, Harris county, narrowly escaped destruction by fire a few days ago.

The Thomasville Enterprise states that Superintendent R. G. Flemning, Assistant Superintendent F. Predergast, Col. C. D. Owens, and James L. Taylor, General Freight Agent of the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway, were in town Friday morning on their way to Bainbridge. On their return they reported the preliminary survey from Bainbridge to Chattahoochee finished, and that the work of locating the line will proceed as rapidly as possible.

A charter has been obtained and a strong company organized to cut a large ditch on the east side of Chestatee river, North Georgia. Professor Ben Hall has made one or more preliminary surveys and finds the route altogether practicable. Though it will be over twenty miles long and built at a pretty heavy outlay of money, yet it will open up a new gold field and develop some of the richest gold mines in the country when completed. The Chestatee will be diverted from its channel some twelve miles above Dahlonega, and the ditch will pass near the celebrated Loud mine and Captain Ashbury, and then along the divide with the Chestatee on the west and the Wahoo and Yellow creek on the east. It will pass through a gold region in its whole length, but the last ten miles, from Shade Conady's to Martin's ford, is considered the new and rich field.

The County Commissioners of Bibb have resolved to issue no more licenses for the sale of liquor outside the limits of Macon.

Ed. Wilson, a thirteen year old colored boy, of Macon, has been detected in stealing small packages from the Southern Express office in that city. His father has been a porter in the company for thirty years. The boy had stolen about $100 worth of property.

Two distineries were seized in Gilmer county last week by Deputies Witt and Hittzdraw and two thousand gallons of beer destroyed.

Two negroes fell out over a game of cards in a McDonough street den in Atlanta on Tuesday and exchanged seven shots. One received an ugly wound in the arm. The other was unhurt.

Jack Morris, colored, was going down a well in a bucket, on Tuesday, in Atlanta. When half way down the windlass broke, and he was knocked senseless by the fall. His injuries are thought to be fatal.

A postal card was intercepted at the New York postoffice, directed "President Arthur, Washington, D. C." Upon the lower left hand corner was written, with a lead pencil, the word "Private." On the reverse was written:

"President Arthur:—If you do not recall the Minister from England and ask for the unconditional surrender of all Americans in English dungeons you shall be shot and killed."

Across these penned lines was written, with a black lead pencil:

"This is no idle boast. We mean business. You are no American."

It caused considerable excitement, but it is probably much more harmless than it was intended to appear and is only a stupid joke.

The stock reporter of the New York Times is a lady, Miss Mary Morgan, who has accumulated a handsome competency by her connection with the Times and Herald, to both of which she furnish reports of the live stock markets. She came to this country about fifteen years ago, and is an expert in all matters relating to cows, sheep, hogs, horses, and can tell the weight of a horned creature at a glance. Her knowledge of horses proved useful to her as a member of Victor Emanuel's staff, as she was intrusted with the duty of buying the horses for his army. At five o'clock in the morning she goes to the stock yards to make out her reports. Miss Morgan is not at all masculine as one might think by her occupation, she is an excellent Italian, French and German scholar, and an accomplished woman, and is highly respected by all who know her.

MRS. BELVA LOCKWOOD, of Washington, the woman lawyer, every morning rides down Pennsylvania Avenue on a tricycle. Her plan to save car fare is novel and attracts much attention. Dr. Mary Walker, another noted female at the capital, has obtained a position in one of the Departments. There is no other lady in the room, and it is said the gentlemen make no exception in her case, saying if she desires those courtesies shown her sex she must change her attire.

Mrs. Bassett, of Philadelphia, says she is the only surviving child of Robert Lewis, who was the son of Fielding Lewis and Betty Lewis, his wife, the only sister of Gen. George Washington. Mrs. Bassett has signified her willingness and desire that Congress should purchase the bible. The matter has been discussed in Congress.

Of these Kirkwood and Porter claim to be revenue reformers, though it is foreseen they incline towards protection. The others are avowed protectionists.

MAJ. B. F. LOGAN, Deputy Sheriff of Cleveland county, was violently assailed in Shelby, by a negro man named Canless Blair. The negro was fleeing from Sheriff Suttles and posse, who were trying to capture him, and as he came near the Major, drew a pistol and fired, the ball hitting a colored man, George Wright, who was standing by. Maj. Logan had a rifle and fired at the negro, the ball entering the shoulder blade. The Major and the negro grappled and both fell to the ground, when the wounded man, Wright, clubbed Blair with his rifle. Maj. Logan released his hold and Blair attempted to run, but two shots from the rifle by the deputy Sheriff, soon disabled him; one entered the thigh, the other his right foot. Blair was placed in jail and confessed to several robberies in and around Shelby. He had been sent to the Penitentiary and escaped from the Railroad guards a few weeks ago. Maj. Logan was not injured in the affray, and the negro man Wright, not seriously hurt—the ball lodged in his leg and was extracted by the surgeon.

The astronomers that went from Europe to Africa and Asia to observe the eclipse of the sun last week, announce positively that during the eclipse they were enabled to clearly make out an atmosphere on the moon. The theory all along has been that no atmosphere exists around the moon and therefore animal life, such as is known to man on this globe cannot exist on the moon; but now that the fact has been established that an atmosphere does exist on the moon, the conclusion is that animal life also exists there.
